claim: 85 male adult mice were used in the study.
source: 85 male adult mice were used.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section under Animals.

claim: The mice used were a cross between DAT (Slc6a3)-Cre mice and tdTomato mice.
source: These mice were the result of a cross between DAT (Slc6a3)-Cre mice (recombinase under the control of the dopamine transporter, DAT) (B6.SJL-Slc6a3tm1.1(cre)Bkmn/J, Jackson Laboratory; RRID:IMSR_JAX:006660) (Bäckman et al., 2006) and tdTomato mice such that they were heterozygous for DAT-Cre and also heterozygous for tdTomato (Gt(ROSA)26Sortm9(CAGtdTomato)Hze, Jackson Laboratory).
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section under Animals, with citation to Bäckman et al., 2006.

claim: Animals were housed on a 12 hr dark/12 hr light cycle with dark from 07:00 to 19:00.
source: Animals were housed on a 12 hr dark/12 hr light cycle (dark from 07:00 to 19:00), one to a cage, and performed the task at the same time each day.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section under Animals.

claim: All procedures were performed in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and approved by the Harvard Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All procedures were performed in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and approved by the Harvard Animal Care and Use Committee.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section under Animals.

claim: AAV5-CAG-FLEX-GCaMP6m virus was injected into both the VTA and SNc to express GCaMP specifically in dopamine neurons.
source: To express GCaMP specifically in dopamine neurons, we unilaterally injected 250 nl of AAV5-CAG-FLEX-GCaMP6m (1 × 1012 particles/ml, Penn Vector Core) into both the VTA and SNc (500 nl total).
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section under Viral injections, fiber implants, and head-plate installation.

claim: Optic fibers were implanted into VS, DMS, DLS, and TS regions of the striatum.
source: Finally, during the same surgery, we also implanted optic fibers into the VS, DMS, DLS, and TS (1–4 fibers per mouse).
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section under Viral injections, fiber implants, and head-plate installation.

claim: 65 fibers total were recorded from, targeted to either VS (n = 25), DMS (n = 8), DLS (n = 8), or TS (n = 24).
source: We recorded from 65 fibers total, targeted to either VS (n = 25), DMS (n = 8), DLS (n = 8), or TS (n = 24) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section under Recording activity from dopamine axons in the striatum.

claim: TS dopamine showed significant excitation above baseline following the presentation of novel odors (p = 1.76x10−6, t-test, n = 12 animals).
source: TS dopamine showed significant excitation above baseline following the presentation of novel odors (p = 1.76x10−6, t-test, n = 12 animals, Figure 2G)
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Excitation to novel cues in TS dopamine.

claim: VS dopamine responses to novel odors were not significantly different from baseline (p = 0.354, t-test, n = 13 animals).
source: whereas responses to novel odors in VS dopamine were not significantly different from baseline (p = 0.354, t-test, n = 13 animals, Figure 2G).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Excitation to novel cues in TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine responses to novel odors decreased significantly over the course of the first 30 odor presentations (p = 5.10x10−11, repeated measures ANOVA, n = 12 animals).
source: The responses to novel odors in TS dopamine decreased significantly over the course of the first 30 odor presentations (p = 5.10x10−11, repeated measures ANOVA, n = 12 animals, Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Excitation to novel cues in TS dopamine.

claim: The responses to novel odors in TS dopamine after five odor representations (6–10 trials) were significantly smaller than the responses in the first five trials (p = 1.45x10−4, paired t-test, n = 12 animals).
source: The responses after five odor representations (6–10 trials) were significantly smaller than the responses in the first five trials (p = 1.45x10−4, paired t-test, n = 12 animals).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Excitation to novel cues in TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine responses to novel odors that predicted water were significantly larger than responses to unpredicted water itself (p = 1.36x10−4, paired t-test, n = 19 animals).
source: The responses to novel odors that predicted water were significantly larger than responses to unpredicted water itself (p = 1.36x10−4, paired t-test, n = 19 animals, Figure 3B).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine responses to odors gradually decreased over 21 days (p = 1.095x10−8, n = 19 animals, repeated measures ANOVA).
source: Dopamine responses to odors gradually decreased over 21 days (p = 1.095x10−8, n = 19 animals, repeated measures ANOVA).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine responses to water-predicting odors were significantly smaller on the seventh day of training than on the first day (p = 1.93x10−5, n = 19 animals, day 1 vs day 7).
source: The responses to water-predicting odors in TS dopamine were significantly smaller on the seventh day of training than on the first day (p = 1.93x10−5, n = 19 animals, day 1 vs day 7, Figure 3B).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine responses to predicted water did not change significantly from day 1 to day 7 (p = 0.641 paired t-test, n = 19 animals).
source: On the other hand, responses to predicted water did not change significantly (p = 0.641 paired t-test, n = 19 animals, day 1 vs day 7, Figure 3B).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: VS dopamine responses to predicted water (US responses) significantly decreased over the course of the first 7 days (p = 1.96x10−4, paired t-test, n = 10 animals).
source: Over the course of the first 7 days, responses to predicted water (US responses) significantly decreased (p = 1.96x10−4, paired t-test, n = 10 animals, Figure 3A).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: VS dopamine did not display significant responses to odor cues that predicted reward on the first day (p = 0.099, t-test, n = 10 animals, CS responses compared to baseline on day 1).
source: VS dopamine did not display significant responses to odor cues that predicted reward on the first day (p = 0.099, t-test, n = 10 animals, CS responses compared to baseline on day 1)
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: VS dopamine did not display significant responses to odor cues that predicted reward on day 7 (p = 0.054, t-test, n = 10 animals, CS responses compared to baseline on day 7).
source: or on day 7 (p = 0.054, t-test, n = 10 animals, CS responses compared to baseline on day 7) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: Anticipatory licking gradually increased in frequency over the course of learning (p = 0.0052, repeated measures ANOVA, n = 10 animals).
source: Anticipatory licking gradually increased in frequency over the course of learning (p = 0.0052, repeated measures ANOVA, n = 10 animals, Figure 3C).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: VS dopamine did not respond to new odors in trained mice (p = 0.8749, t-test, n = 9 animals, trial one or p = 0.322, t-test, n = 9 animals, trial 1–5 vs baseline).
source: VS dopamine did not respond to new odors (p = 0.8749, t-test, n = 9 animals, trial one or p = 0.322, t-test, n = 9 animals, trial 1–5 vs baseline, Figure 4B–E)
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine strongly responded to new odors in trained mice (p = 0.0059, t-test, n = 11 animals, trial one or p = 0.0027, t-test, n = 11 animals, trial 1–5 vs baseline).
source: and TS dopamine strongly responded to new odors (p = 0.0059, t-test, n = 11 animals, trial one or p = 0.0027, t-test, n = 11 animals, trial 1–5 vs baseline, Figure 4H–K).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine showed excitation to 91% of new odor presentations (response in trial one vs baseline).
source: Indeed, TS dopamine showed excitation to 91% of new odor presentations (response in trial one vs baseline).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: Anticipatory licking in response to the rewarded odor increased after a few trials (p = 0.0387, paired t-test, n = 20 animals, trial 1–5 water CS lick vs baseline).
source: Anticipatory licking in response to the rewarded odor increased after a few trials (p = 0.0387, paired t-test, n = 20 animals, trial 1–5 water CS lick vs baseline) (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: Animals showed differences in anticipatory licking frequency depending on cues within 10 trials of training (p = 0.000259, paired t-test, n = 20 animals, trial 6–10 water CS lick vs nothing CS lick).
source: The animals showed differences in anticipatory licking frequency depending on cues within 10 trials of training (p = 0.000259, paired t-test, n = 20 animals, trial 6–10 water CS lick vs nothing CS lick), indicating learning of the outcomes of the odor cue (Figure 5C).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: VS dopamine did not show differences in responses to cues before 15 trials (p = 0.7736, paired t-test, n = 9 animals, water CS vs nothing CS trial 11–15).
source: VS dopamine did not show differences in responses to cues before 15 trials (p = 0.7736, paired t-test, n = 9 animals, water CS vs nothing CS trial 11–15, Figure 5D)
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: VS dopamine responses to predicted water decreased quickly (p = 0.020, paired t-test, n = 9 animals, trial 1–5 vs 6–10).
source: whereas responses to predicted water decreased quickly (p = 0.020, paired t-test, n = 9 animals, trial 1–5 vs 6–10, Figure 5E).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine decreased responses to cues depending on what the cue predicted within five trials (p = 0.0213, paired t-test, n = 11 animals, water CS vs nothing CS trial 1–5).
source: TS dopamine decreased responses to cues depending on what the cue predicted within five trials (p = 0.0213, paired t-test, n = 11 animals, water CS vs nothing CS trial 1–5, Figure 5D)
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: The median onset latency of responses to novel odors in TS dopamine was 140 ms.
source: The median onset latency of responses to novel odors in TS dopamine was 140 ms (Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: The median onset latency of discrimination between novel odors and familiar odors in TS dopamine was 170 ms.
source: and the median onset latency of discrimination between novel odors and familiar odors in TS dopamine was 170 ms (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: Both VS and TS dopamine had a larger excitatory response to reward-predicting cues than cues predicting nothing (VS: p = 1.8x10−10, TS: p = 6.5x10−6, t-test).
source: With respect to reward prediction, both VS and TS dopamine had a larger excitatory response to reward-predicting cues than cues predicting nothing (VS: p = 1.8x10−10, TS: p = 6.5x10−6, t-test, Figure 6A,D).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Responses to rewarding and non-rewarding stimuli in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: Both VS and TS dopamine had a smaller response to a predicted reward than an unpredicted reward (VS: p = 5.1x10−11, TS: p = 1.0x10−4, t-test).
source: Similarly, both VS and TS dopamine had a smaller response to a predicted reward than an unpredicted reward (VS: p = 5.1x10−11, TS: p = 1.0x10−4, t-test, Figure 6A,D).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Responses to rewarding and non-rewarding stimuli in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: VS dopamine showed a dip below baseline following reward omission (VS: p = 4.8x10−7, t-test).
source: However, there was a significant difference in the response to the omission of a predicted reward: whereas VS dopamine showed a dip below baseline following reward omission (VS: p = 4.8x10−7, t-test, Figure 6A,D)
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Responses to rewarding and non-rewarding stimuli in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine axon signal was significantly higher than baseline following reward omission (p = 2.2x10−8, t-test).
source: TS dopamine axon signal was still significantly higher than baseline following omission (p = 2.2x10−8, t-test, Figure 6A,D).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Responses to rewarding and non-rewarding stimuli in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine showed less excitation to predicted air puff or tone than unpredicted air puff or tone (p = 0.00016, p = 0.00074).
source: For example, TS dopamine showed less excitation to predicted air puff or tone than unpredicted air puff or tone (p = 0.00016, p = 0.00074, Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Responses to rewarding and non-rewarding stimuli in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine cue responses to air puff or tone predicting cues were larger than the responses to cues predicting no outcome (air puff: p = 6.8x10−4, tone: p = 3.4x10−4).
source: Additionally, TS dopamine cue responses to air puff or tone predicting cues were larger than the responses to cues predicting no outcome (air puff: p = 6.8x10−4, tone: p = 3.4x10−4, Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Responses to rewarding and non-rewarding stimuli in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: Novelty responses were correlated with location along the anterior-posterior axis (r = −0.92, p = 1.68x10−9, n = 40 animals, Pearson's correlation).
source: Novelty responses were correlated with location along the anterior-posterior axis (r = −0.92, p = 1.68x10−9, n = 40 animals, Pearson's correlation).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Organization of dopamine novelty responses in VS and TS.

claim: Responses to water, nothing, air puff, and omission were correlated with the location along anterior-posterior axis (water: r = 0.61, p = 5.76x10−5, nothing: r = −0.16, p = 2.61x10−7, air puff: r = −0.76, p = 4.58x10−8, and omission: r = −0.38, p = 1.68x10−9, n = 40 animals).
source: Responses for all these factors were correlated with the location along anterior-posterior axis to various degrees (water: r = 0.61, p = 5.76x10−5, nothing: r = −0.16, p = 2.61x10−7, air puff: r = −0.76, p = 4.58x10−8, and omission: r = −0.38, p = 1.68x10−9, n = 40 animals).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Organization of dopamine novelty responses in VS and TS.

claim: Novelty responses were positively correlated with responses to nothing, air puff-predicting cues, and reward omission (nothing: p = 8.76x10−7, air puff: p = 1.01x10−14, omission: p = 9.02x10−10, n = 40 animals).
source: Finally, novelty responses were positively correlated with responses to nothing, air puff-predicting cues, and reward omission (nothing: p = 8.76x10−7, air puff: p = 1.01x10−14, omission: p = 9.02x10−10, n = 40 animals).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Organization of dopamine novelty responses in VS and TS.

claim: Water responses were slightly anti-correlated with novelty responses (p = 0.0138, n = 40 animals).
source: By contrast, water responses were observed in both VS and TS, although the amplitudes of water responses were slightly anti-correlated with novelty responses (p = 0.0138, n = 40 animals).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Organization of dopamine novelty responses in VS and TS.

claim: Dopamine neurons are thought to encode novelty in addition to reward prediction error.
source: Dopamine neurons are thought to encode novelty in addition to reward prediction error (the discrepancy between actual and predicted values).
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as background knowledge.

claim: During classical conditioning, opposite dynamics were observed in dopamine axon signals in the ventral striatum and the posterior tail of the striatum.
source: During classical conditioning, we observed opposite dynamics in dopamine axon signals in the ventral striatum ('VS dopamine') and the posterior tail of the striatum ('TS dopamine').
evidence: Main finding stated in the Abstract.

claim: TS dopamine showed strong excitation to novel cues.
source: TS dopamine showed strong excitation to novel cues, whereas VS dopamine showed no responses to novel cues until they had been paired with a reward.
evidence: Main finding stated in the Abstract.

claim: VS dopamine showed no responses to novel cues until they had been paired with a reward.
source: TS dopamine showed strong excitation to novel cues, whereas VS dopamine showed no responses to novel cues until they had been paired with a reward.
evidence: Main finding stated in the Abstract.

claim: TS dopamine cue responses decreased over time, depending on what the cue predicted.
source: TS dopamine cue responses decreased over time, depending on what the cue predicted.
evidence: Main finding stated in the Abstract.

claim: TS dopamine showed excitation to several types of stimuli including rewarding, aversive, and neutral stimuli.
source: Additionally, TS dopamine showed excitation to several types of stimuli including rewarding, aversive, and neutral stimuli whereas VS dopamine showed excitation only to reward or reward-predicting cues.
evidence: Main finding stated in the Abstract.

claim: VS dopamine showed excitation only to reward or reward-predicting cues.
source: Additionally, TS dopamine showed excitation to several types of stimuli including rewarding, aversive, and neutral stimuli whereas VS dopamine showed excitation only to reward or reward-predicting cues.
evidence: Main finding stated in the Abstract.

claim: Dopamine novelty signals are localized in TS along with general salience signals.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that dopamine novelty signals are localized in TS along with general salience signals, while VS dopamine reliably encodes reward prediction error.
evidence: Main conclusion stated in the Abstract.

claim: VS dopamine reliably encodes reward prediction error.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that dopamine novelty signals are localized in TS along with general salience signals, while VS dopamine reliably encodes reward prediction error.
evidence: Main conclusion stated in the Abstract.

claim: Detection of novel stimuli is advantageous for survival because novel stimuli can signal potential rewards or potential threats.
source: Detection of novel stimuli is advantageous for survival because novel stimuli can signal potential rewards or potential threats.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as background knowledge.

claim: Novelty detection is fundamental for computation in our brain.
source: In addition to behavioral advantages, novelty detection is fundamental for computation in our brain.
evidence: Stated in the Introduction as background knowledge.

claim: Behavioral studies have repeatedly shown that both humans and other animals have enhanced memory for novel items.
source: Indeed, behavioral studies have repeatedly shown that both humans and other animals have enhanced memory for novel items (Kishiyama et al., 2009; Restorff, 1933).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to Kishiyama et al., 2009 and Restorff, 1933.

claim: Single unit recordings have shown that dopamine neurons in the midbrain increase their firing in response to the presentation of a novel stimulus in several species and behavioral paradigms.
source: Among these, single unit recordings have shown that dopamine neurons in the midbrain increase their firing in response to the presentation of a novel stimulus in several species and behavioral paradigms (Horvitz et al., 1997; Ljungberg et al., 1992; Schultz, 2015; Steinfels et al., 1983).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to Horvitz et al., 1997; Ljungberg et al., 1992; Schultz, 2015; Steinfels et al., 1983.

claim: Dopamine neurons are thought to be the neural substrate underlying associative learning because they signal reward prediction error.
source: Dopamine neurons are thought to be the neural substrate underlying this type of learning because they signal reward prediction error: the difference between actual and expected reward values (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Clark et al., 2012; Cohen et al., 2012; Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Clark et al., 2012; Cohen et al., 2012; Schultz et al., 1997.

claim: Dopamine neurons are thought to guide decision-making by broadcasting reward prediction error information to many regions of the forebrain and reinforcing behaviors that lead to reward.
source: These neurons are thought to guide decision-making by broadcasting this information to many regions of the forebrain and reinforcing behaviors that lead to reward (Barto et al., 1999; Dayan and Niv, 2008; Haber, 2014; Montague et al., 2004; Steinberg et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to Barto et al., 1999; Dayan and Niv, 2008; Haber, 2014; Montague et al., 2004; Steinberg et al., 2013.

claim: One hypothesis was that dopamine neurons take an optimistic approach toward novel stimuli, assuming that they will predict a valuable outcome until proven wrong.
source: One hypothesis was that dopamine neurons take an optimistic approach toward novel stimuli, assuming that they will predict a valuable outcome until proven wrong (Hazy et al., 2010; Kakade and Dayan, 2002).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to Hazy et al., 2010; Kakade and Dayan, 2002.

claim: Recent studies have shown that there is substantial diversity among dopamine neurons at the molecular level.
source: Recent studies have shown that there is substantial diversity among dopamine neurons at the molecular level (Grimm et al., 2004; Lacey et al., 1989; Lammel et al., 2008; Roeper, 2013) as well as in their activity (Brischoux et al., 2009; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to Grimm et al., 2004; Lacey et al., 1989; Lammel et al., 2008; Roeper, 2013; Brischoux et al., 2009; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010.

claim: Single unit recordings in monkeys showed that some dopamine neurons are inhibited by aversive outcomes and others are excited by them.
source: For example, single unit recordings in monkeys showed that some dopamine neurons are inhibited by aversive outcomes and others are excited by them (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citation to Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009.

claim: Dopamine neurons with different projection targets receive different inputs.
source: More recent studies have shown that dopamine neurons with different projection targets receive different inputs (Beier et al., 2015; Lerner et al., 2015; Menegas et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citations to Beier et al., 2015; Lerner et al., 2015; Menegas et al., 2015.

claim: Dopamine neurons projecting to the posterior 'tail' of the striatum (TS) have unique inputs compared to dopamine neurons projecting to many other brain regions, including the ventral striatum (VS).
source: Specifically, we found that dopamine neurons projecting to the posterior 'tail' of the striatum (TS) have unique inputs compared to dopamine neurons projecting to many other brain regions, including the ventral striatum (VS), suggesting that these neurons could have a distinct function (Menegas et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in the Introduction with citation to Menegas et al., 2015.

claim: Novelty responses in dopamine may be better formalized separately from the reward prediction error (RPE) framework, rather than being included in the RPE framework.
source: Thus, novelty responses in dopamine may be better formalized separately from the reward prediction error (RPE) framework, rather than being included in the RPE framework.
evidence: Main conclusion stated in the Introduction.

claim: Fiber photometry allows for recording of the activity of genetically defined neural populations in behaving mice by expressing a genetically encoded Ca2+ indicator, GCaMP6m.
source: Fiber fluorometry (photometry) (Kudo et al., 1992) allows for recording of the activity of genetically defined neural populations in behaving mice by expressing a genetically encoded Ca2+ indicator, GCaMP6m (Akerboom et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013) and chronically implanting an optic fiber.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section under Fiber fluorometry with citations to Kudo et al., 1992; Akerboom et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013.

claim: Mice licked with an increased frequency in response to the reward-predicting odor after training.
source: After training, mice licked with an increased frequency in response to the reward-predicting odor (anticipating the reward), but not in response to odors that predicted no outcome (Figure 1D), indicating that mice had learned an association between an odor and reward.
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Recording activity from dopamine axons in the striatum.

claim: Large responses to unpredicted reward were observed in GCaMP, but not tdTomato, signals.
source: We observed large responses to unpredicted reward in GCaMP, but not tdTomato, signals (example traces shown in Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Recording activity from dopamine axons in the striatum.

claim: Recordings from the same fibers were stable over the course of several weeks.
source: and recorded from the same fibers over the course of several weeks with relative stability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Recording activity from dopamine axons in the striatum.

claim: Brains were cleared using CLARITY, imaged as intact volumes using a light sheet microscope, and aligned to a single reference space to identify fiber implant sites.
source: We identified the fiber implant sites by clearing brains using CLARITY (Chung and Deisseroth, 2013), imaging them as intact volumes using a light sheet microscope (Tomer et al., 2014), and aligning them to a single reference space (Menegas et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Recording activity from dopamine axons in the striatum with citations to Chung and Deisseroth, 2013; Tomer et al., 2014; Menegas et al., 2015.

claim: Mice did not show major body movements in response to odors predicting no outcome or novel odors.
source: We found that mice did not show major body movements in response to odors predicting no outcome (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B) or novel odors (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), although they performed a stereotypical approach behavior in response to odors predicting reward (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Excitation to novel cues in TS dopamine.

claim: Both VS dopamine responses and TS dopamine responses to free water remained constant within sessions.
source: We found that both VS dopamine responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and TS dopamine responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) to free water remained constant within sessions.
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Excitation to novel cues in TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine responses to familiar odors predicting no reward remained constant within sessions.
source: Similarly, TS dopamine responses to familiar odors predicting no reward remained constant as well (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Excitation to novel cues in TS dopamine.

claim: Mice behaviorally responded to reward-predicting odors faster than VS dopamine CS responses developed.
source: Plotting the CS and US responses as a function of anticipatory licks (rather than time) showed that mice behaviorally responded to reward-predicting odors faster than VS dopamine CS responses developed, while TS dopamine CS responses were present in all trials (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine CS responses were present in all trials during learning.
source: Plotting the CS and US responses as a function of anticipatory licks (rather than time) showed that mice behaviorally responded to reward-predicting odors faster than VS dopamine CS responses developed, while TS dopamine CS responses were present in all trials (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: In TS, reward prediction elicited sustained activity over the interval between odor presentation and reward onset, and reward delivery caused only a small increase above this level.
source: In TS, reward prediction elicited sustained activity over the interval between odor presentation and reward onset, and reward delivery caused only a small increase above this level.
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Responses to rewarding and non-rewarding stimuli in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: In TS dopamine, the average peak response was slightly higher in rewarded trials than unrewarded trials (p = 0.0014).
source: In fact, although the average peak response was slightly higher in rewarded trials than unrewarded trials (p = 0.0014), the total response (area under each curve) after the outcome (reward delivery or omission) did not differ significantly (p = 0.81).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Responses to rewarding and non-rewarding stimuli in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: In TS dopamine, the total response (area under each curve) after the outcome (reward delivery or omission) did not differ significantly (p = 0.81).
source: In fact, although the average peak response was slightly higher in rewarded trials than unrewarded trials (p = 0.0014), the total response (area under each curve) after the outcome (reward delivery or omission) did not differ significantly (p = 0.81).
evidence: Statistical test result directly stated in the Results section under Responses to rewarding and non-rewarding stimuli in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: The omission of an expected tone or expected air puff did not cause a dip or increase in TS dopamine signal.
source: Similar to water omission, the omission of an expected tone or expected air puff did not cause a dip or increase in signal (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Responses to rewarding and non-rewarding stimuli in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: VS dopamine encodes RPE whereas TS dopamine responds to salient stimuli in general.
source: In summary, VS dopamine encodes RPE whereas TS dopamine responds to salient stimuli in general.
evidence: Summary statement in the Results section under Responses to rewarding and non-rewarding stimuli in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: TS dopamine encodes the prediction of salient stimuli, and decreases the responses to salient stimuli once they are predicted, which are characteristics of prediction error.
source: TS dopamine encodes the prediction of salient stimuli, and decreases the responses to salient stimuli once they are predicted, which are characteristics of prediction error.
evidence: Summary statement in the Results section under Responses to rewarding and non-rewarding stimuli in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: No systematic differences of novelty responses were observed along dorsal-ventral or medial-lateral axis within VS.
source: We did not observe systematic differences of novelty responses along dorsal-ventral or medial-lateral axis within VS (Figure 7A, anterior), although our spatial resolution could not completely distinguish each sub-nucleus.
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Organization of dopamine novelty responses in VS and TS.

claim: No noticeable differences between novelty responses in different sub-regions of TS were observed.
source: We did not observe noticeable differences between novelty responses in different sub-regions of TS either (Figure 7A, posterior).
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Organization of dopamine novelty responses in VS and TS.

claim: Water responses were found in all parts of the striatum.
source: We observed that water responses were found in all parts of the striatum (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in the Results section under Organization of dopamine novelty responses in VS and TS.

claim: The differences in novelty responses and value coding between VS and TS dopamine suggest that novelty responses and value coding in dopamine axons are at least partially segregated in the striatum.
source: Together, the differences in novelty responses and value coding between VS and TS dopamine suggested that novelty responses and value coding in dopamine axons are at least partially segregated in the striatum; lack of inhibitory responses to reward omission and excitatory responses to neutral or aversive stimulus are localized in TS and coincide with excitatory responses to novel stimuli.
evidence: Summary statement in the Results section under Organization of dopamine novelty responses in VS and TS.

claim: Lack of inhibitory responses to reward omission and excitatory responses to neutral or aversive stimulus are localized in TS and coincide with excitatory responses to novel stimuli.
source: Together, the differences in novelty responses and value coding between VS and TS dopamine suggested that novelty responses and value coding in dopamine axons are at least partially segregated in the striatum; lack of inhibitory responses to reward omission and excitatory responses to neutral or aversive stimulus are localized in TS and coincide with excitatory responses to novel stimuli.
evidence: Summary statement in the Results section under Organization of dopamine novelty responses in VS and TS.

claim: Dopamine neurons that project to the TS are anatomical outliers compared to many other dopamine neurons including dopamine neurons that project to the VS.
source: Our previous study showed that dopamine neurons that project to the TS are anatomical outliers compared to many other dopamine neurons including dopamine neurons that project to the VS (Menegas et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine with citation to Menegas et al., 2015.

claim: Dopamine neurons that project to TS are not only anatomically, but also functionally, distinct compared to dopamine neurons that project to VS.
source: These new results suggest that dopamine neurons that project to TS are not only anatomically, but also functionally, distinct compared to dopamine neurons that project to VS.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: The novelty responses observed in TS dopamine, and especially the lack of novelty responses in VS dopamine, stand in stark contrast to popular theories explaining how novelty responses could fit into the dopamine RPE framework.
source: The novelty responses we observed in TS dopamine, and especially the lack of novelty responses in VS dopamine, stand in stark contrast to popular theories explaining how novelty responses could fit into the dopamine RPE framework (Hazy et al., 2010; Kakade and Dayan, 2002).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine with citations to Hazy et al., 2010; Kakade and Dayan, 2002.

claim: The 'pure value'-coding VS dopamine axon signal does not include a novelty response, while the salience-coding TS dopamine axon signal does include a novelty response.
source: However, our results suggest that the 'pure value'-coding VS dopamine axon signal does not include a novelty response, while the salience-coding TS dopamine axon signal does include a novelty response.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: CS-value in VS dopamine was initialized with no value, while CS-salience in TS dopamine was initialized with very high salience.
source: These dynamics can be conceptualized such that CS-value in VS dopamine was initialized with no value, while CS-salience in TS dopamine was initialized with very high salience.
evidence: Interpretation stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: Dopamine dynamics in VS are well suited to serve as US associability, the teaching signal of the Rescorla-Wagner model.
source: Dopamine dynamics in VS are well suited to serve as US associability, the teaching signal of the Rescorla-Wagner model (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972).
evidence: Interpretation stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine with citation to Rescorla and Wagner, 1972.

claim: TS dopamine does not follow the dynamics that the Rescola-Wagner model predicts.
source: TS dopamine does not follow the dynamics that the Rescola-Wagner model predicts.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: The dynamics of TS dopamine suggest that they may serve as CS associability, providing the attention signals for learning.
source: The dynamics of TS dopamine suggest that they may serve as CS associability, providing the attention signals for learning.
evidence: Interpretation stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: CS associability, or the 'attention' term in dopamine signals may not be an exception in RPE, but instead may be a separate system – localized in particular brain regions such as in TS.
source: Here, we propose that CS associability, or the 'attention' term in dopamine signals may not be an exception in RPE, but instead may be a separate system – localized in particular brain regions such as in TS.
evidence: Proposal stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: Dopamine in TS signals novelty and salience, and dopamine in VS signals RPE, although both systems may co-exist in some brain areas.
source: Thus, dopamine in TS signals novelty and salience, and dopamine in VS signals RPE, although both systems may co-exist in some brain areas.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: Attention would be critical to reduce the amount of information for learning to a more realistic amount.
source: Attention would be critical to reduce the amount of information for learning to a more realistic amount.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: Dopamine in TS may be specialized for the function of reducing information for learning.
source: Dopamine in TS may be specialized for this function.
evidence: Speculation stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: A recent study suggested that putative dopamine neurons in lateral SNc in monkey represented 'cognitive salience', which was correlated with working memory load.
source: In line with this idea, a recent study suggested that putative dopamine neurons in lateral SNc in monkey represented 'cognitive salience', which was correlated with working memory load (Matsumoto and Takada, 2013).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine with citation to Matsumoto and Takada, 2013.

claim: Previous studies suggested that SNc is important for the acquisition of enhanced CS associability.
source: Behaviorally, previous studies suggested that SNc is important for the acquisition of enhanced CS associability (Lee et al., 2008, 2006).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine with citations to Lee et al., 2008, 2006.

claim: Dopamine in the prefrontal cortex has been modeled to serve a 'gating' function to provide flexible updating in working memory.
source: Mechanistically, dopamine in the prefrontal cortex has been modeled to serve a 'gating' function to provide flexible updating in working memory (Braver and Cohen, 1999), and a similar mechanism may apply to dopamine in TS.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine with citation to Braver and Cohen, 1999.

claim: TS, categorized in caudal extreme, does not receive projections from sensorimotor cortex, suggesting a functional distinction from other areas in the striatum.
source: Of note, different from adjacent striatal areas, TS, categorized in caudal extreme (Hintiryan et al., 2016), does not receive projections from sensorimotor cortex, suggesting a functional distinction from other areas in the striatum.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine with citation to Hintiryan et al., 2016.

claim: TS dopamine may function to 'pre-process' sensory inputs to weigh potentially important stimuli to make reinforcement learning more efficient in a complex environment.
source: All in all, TS dopamine may function to 'pre-process' sensory inputs to weigh potentially important stimuli to make reinforcement learning more efficient in a complex environment.
evidence: Speculation stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: During the learning of an association between a stimulus and a reward, dopamine signals in VS and TS may cooperate.
source: Thus, during the learning of an association between a stimulus and a reward, dopamine signals in VS and TS may cooperate.
evidence: Speculation stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: Salience prediction error in TS dopamine may serve as the CS associability of the stimulus, whereas value prediction error in VS dopamine may serve as the US associability of the reward.
source: Salience prediction error in TS dopamine may serve as the CS associability of the stimulus, whereas value prediction error in VS dopamine may serve as the US associability of the reward.
evidence: Speculation stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: Salience prediction error in TS dopamine may reinforce stimulus-stimulus associations, similar to value prediction error in VS dopamine during stimulus-reward association.
source: Alternatively, similar to value prediction error in VS dopamine during stimulus-reward association, salience prediction error in TS dopamine may reinforce stimulus-stimulus associations.
evidence: Speculation stated in the Discussion section under Opposite initialization to novel cues in VS and TS dopamine.

claim: The decrease in response to predicted rewards (US) in VS dopamine was faster than the increase in response to reward-predicting odors (CS), occurring over the course of a single session versus weeks of training.
source: In VS, the decrease in response to predicted rewards (US) was faster, occurring over the course of a single session, whereas the increase in response to reward-predicting odors (CS) required weeks of training.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Different time-courses of CS and US responses in dopamine axons during learning.

claim: The development of CS responses in VS dopamine was much slower than the associative learning observed at the behavioral level.
source: The development of CS responses in VS dopamine was also much slower than the associative learning observed at the behavioral level.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Different time-courses of CS and US responses in dopamine axons during learning.

claim: US responses in VS dopamine decreased as anticipatory licking increased.
source: By contrast, US responses decreased as anticipatory licking increased.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Different time-courses of CS and US responses in dopamine axons during learning.

claim: US responses in VS dopamine are well suited as prediction error signals in the Rescorla-Wagner learning model, whereas CS responses are not time-locked to this learning.
source: These results demonstrate that US responses in VS dopamine are well suited as prediction error signals in the Rescorla-Wagner learning model, whereas CS responses are not time-locked to this learning.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the Discussion section under Different time-courses of CS and US responses in dopamine axons during learning.

claim: The time course of CS responses observed in VS dopamine is not easily explained by simple TD models.
source: The time course of CS responses we observed in VS dopamine is not easily explained by simple TD models.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Different time-courses of CS and US responses in dopamine axons during learning.

claim: Distinct mechanisms could cause VS dopamine excitation in response to a reward-predicting CS and VS dopamine suppression in response to a predicted US.
source: It is possible that distinct mechanisms could cause VS dopamine excitation in response to a reward-predicting CS and VS dopamine suppression in response to a predicted US, as proposed in several previous models (Brown et al., 1999; O'Reilly et al., 2007).
evidence: Speculation stated in the Discussion section under Different time-courses of CS and US responses in dopamine axons during learning with citations to Brown et al., 1999; O'Reilly et al., 2007.

claim: Dopamine activity in VTA and dopamine in the ventral striatum increased in novel environments.
source: It has been reported that dopamine activity in VTA and dopamine in the ventral striatum increased in the former case, in novel environments (Segovia et al., 2010; Takeuchi et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies with citations to Segovia et al., 2010; Takeuchi et al., 2016.

claim: Different brain areas are responsible for different kinds of novelty.
source: Interestingly, previous studies found that different brain areas are responsible for different kinds of novelty (Schomaker and Meeter, 2015).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies with citation to Schomaker and Meeter, 2015.

claim: Dopamine neurons that project to TS were mainly observed in the lateral SNc of mice.
source: In our previous study, dopamine neurons that project to TS were mainly observed in the lateral SNc of mice (Menegas et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies with citation to Menegas et al., 2015.

claim: A previous study proposed that putative dopamine neurons in the lateral SNc of monkeys encode 'motivational salience', which is the absolute value of positive or negative 'value'.
source: A previous study proposed that putative dopamine neurons in the lateral SNc of monkeys encode 'motivational salience', which is the absolute value of positive or negative 'value' (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies with citation to Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009.

claim: Another study proposed that excitation of dopamine neurons in response to non-rewarding stimuli encodes the stimulus intensity, regardless of value.
source: On the other hand, another study proposed that excitation of dopamine neurons in response to non-rewarding stimuli encodes the stimulus intensity, regardless of value (Fiorillo et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies with citation to Fiorillo et al., 2013.

claim: The excitation of TS dopamine elicited by various neutral stimuli suggests that the responses in TS could be related to more general salience rather than motivational salience.
source: In the present study, the excitation of TS dopamine elicited by various neutral stimuli suggested that the responses in TS could be related to more general salience rather than motivational salience, although we cannot rule out the possibility that the tone and odor predicting nothing had positive or negative motivational values.
evidence: Interpretation stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies.

claim: TS dopamine appears to encode general stimulus salience prediction error, which includes prediction-dependent suppression and prediction.
source: Instead, TS dopamine appears to encode general stimulus salience prediction error, which includes prediction-dependent suppression and prediction.
evidence: Interpretation stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies.

claim: The novelty responses observed may be the extreme case of salience prediction error, causing large excitation because of minimum prediction, rather than an exception.
source: The novelty responses we observed may be the extreme case of salience prediction error, causing large excitation because of minimum prediction, rather than an exception.
evidence: Interpretation stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies.

claim: A recent study found that putative dopamine neurons which project to the tail of the caudate (part of posterior striatum) in monkey formed another group of dopamine neurons that did not respond to water reward but encoded 'sustained values' of visual cues.
source: A recent study found that putative dopamine neurons which project to the tail of the caudate (part of posterior striatum) in monkey formed another group of dopamine neurons. These dopamine neurons did not respond to water reward but encoded 'sustained values' of visual cues, whereas putative dopamine neurons projecting to the anterior caudate encoded 'updating values', when cue-outcome contingency was frequently changed (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies with citation to Kim et al., 2015.

claim: The results indicate that the difference between VS and TS dopamine extends beyond their flexibility.
source: However, our results indicate that the difference between VS and TS dopamine extends beyond their flexibility.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies.

claim: The dynamics between VS and TS dopamine are different in nature, not only in learning speed.
source: The dynamics between them are different in nature, not only in learning speed.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies.

claim: TS dopamine did not encode 'values'.
source: Most importantly, we found that TS dopamine did not encode 'values'.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies.

claim: Behavioral responses to novel odors are very quick, within one respiration cycle in rats.
source: Of note, behavioral responses to novel odors are very quick, within one respiration cycle in rats (Wesson et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies with citation to Wesson et al., 2008.

claim: The responses to novel odors in TS dopamine began within 200 ms, most likely within one respiration cycle.
source: The responses to novel odors in TS dopamine that we observed began within 200 ms, most likely within one respiration cycle, suggesting a potential contribution at the early stages of novelty.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Relation to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies proposed that there is a temporal separation of two signals (stimulus intensity and value) in single dopamine neurons.
source: First, previous studies (Fiorillo et al., 2013; Schultz, 2015) proposed that there is a temporal separation of two signals (stimulus intensity and value) in single dopamine neurons.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Technical considerations with citations to Fiorillo et al., 2013; Schultz, 2015.

claim: The limited temporal resolution of population calcium imaging using GCaMP6m may only allow measurement of the sum of stimulus intensity and value signals.
source: However, we may only be able to measure the sum of these signals because of the limited temporal resolution of our method (population calcium imaging using GCaMP6m).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Technical considerations.

claim: A recent study found that dopamine axons with distinct signals (locomotion and reward) coexist in the dorsal-most part of the dorsal striatum.

source: Dopamine axons passing through and below the ventral striatum to the cortex (Aransay et al., 2014) may have contributed to the signals in VS dopamine, although calcium transients in passing axons are smaller than in axon terminals and boutons (Koester and Sakmann, 2000; Llano et al., 1997).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Technical considerations with citations to Aransay et al., 2014; Koester and Sakmann, 2000; Llano et al., 1997.

claim: The activity of axons of dopamine neurons may not directly correspond to amounts of dopamine release at synapses or spike activities in cell bodies.
source: Finally, the activity of axons of dopamine neurons may not directly correspond to amounts of dopamine release at synapses or spike activities in cell bodies.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Technical considerations.

source: Dopamine neurons that project to the ventral striatum (mainly medial shell) are able to co-release glutamate (Stuber et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Technical considerations with citation to Stuber et al., 2010.

claim: Neuronal activities can be modulated locally at axon terminals in the striatum by cholinergic neurons.
source: Neuronal activities can be modulated locally at axon terminals in the striatum by cholinergic neurons (Threlfell et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section under Technical considerations with citation to Threlfell et al., 2012.

claim: RPE is not contaminated or distorted in VS dopamine.
